rv.q: Smith is a large man and a deeply experienced purveyor of Wilsonian wisdom (Wilson himself used to tell me how much he admired Smith).
Chuck Smith already has a reputation for being one of the foremost interpreters of Wilson's works, and JOE TURNER once again proves that this reputation is both well-earned and firmly secured.
Either way, mine is 'Joe Turner's Come and Gone,' now receiving a big, richly acted revival at the Goodman Theatre.
This is a truly splendid and spellbinding production, certainly one for the ages.
"Joe Turner's Come and Gone" is a truly extraordinary piece of theatre, of storytelling, of the song that resonates for all of us within the human spirit.
What a treat it is to see these works produced to impeccable, if not gold standards complete with dream casting.
It's an explosive performance of a piece with some of Brian Dennehy's best work on this stage.
All of August Wilson's plays are must-sees, and Joe Turner's Come and Gone is stunningly captivating, engaging, and mesmerically displays African Americans' skillful and enduring abilities.
Full of (sometimes literally) shining moments, the show never fully comes together and ends on a murky, irresolute note.
Directed to perfection by Chuck Smith ( a true veteran of translating Wilson's poetic-like stories to the stage) on a set designed by Linda Buchanan that will knock your sox off.
All that said, if you've never seen Joe Turner it is worth seeing.
